Written Answers to [30 July, 2015]   Unstarred Questions 149
Chief Ministers on Rationalization of Centrally Sponsored Schemes was constituted 
on March 9, 2015 to look into the following issues i) To examine the existing 
CSSs and recommend measures for ensuring that their implementation is streamlined 
and adequately flexible; (ii) In light of the Finance Commission recommendations, 
the increased devolution of taxes to States and the higher revenue deficit grants 
to suggest reforms of the Schemes which are being continued under CSSs;  
(iii) To recommend appropriate measures for coordination between the Centre and 
the States and among the States for achieving the objectives of the Schemes;  
(iv) Any other measures related to the schemes to strengthen the national 
development agenda and ensure outcomes. 
Sub-Group of Chief Ministers on Rationalization of Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes is yet to submit its report. In the budget of 2014-15, provisions were 
made for 66 Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) of which 17 were flagship 
Schemes following the restructuring exercise carried out in 2013. However, in 
the budgetary proposal of 2015-16, existing CSSs have been classified into four 
categories. 
Category A:  Centrally Sponsored Schemes placed in this category are proposed 
to be implemented with full Central support.
Category B: Funding pattern of Centrally Sponsored Schemes placed in this 
category are proposed to be changed. 
Category C: Centrally Sponsored Schemes placed in this category are delinked 
from Union support and States may decide to continue or not from their own 
resources. 
Category D:  Schemes placed in this category are part of devolution to the 
States or have been restructured and amalgamated among Schemes in A, B or C. 
Relevant extract of the budgetary proposal of 2015-16 is given in the 
Statement ( See below). 
Following the acceptance of recommendations of the 14th Finance Commission 
of raising the devolution of net tax receipt from 32% to 42%, the fiscal space 
available with Central Government to fund Centrally Sponsored Scheme has been 
reduced.

Revisiting Rangarajan Panel for definition of poverty
1211. SHRIMATI WANSUK SYIEM: Will the Minister of PLANNING be 
pleased to state:
(a) whether new poverty figures thrown up by the recently released data of 
socio-economic and caste census would come handy for the Government to revisit 
the Rangarajan Panel findings and definition of poverty;
(b) whether, according to the Socio-Economic Census 2011, 31.26 per cent rural 
Indians were assessed to be poor while Rangarajan Panel pegged the figure at 30.9 
per cent; and
(c) whether the methodology to assess the depth of poverty by the Socio-
Economic Survey 2011 format was based on landed assets and income whereas the 
Rangarajan Panel took into account Government data on consumption expenditure 
towards food, transport, health and education?
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING  
(RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) The Expert Group under the Chairmanship of  
Dr. C. Rangarajan to ‘Review the Methodology for Measurement of Poverty’ has 
estimated poverty from the Large Sample Surveys on Household Consumer Expenditure 
carried out by the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) of the Ministry of Statistics 
and Programme Implementation. It has based poverty line on certain normative levels of 
adequate nourishment, clothing, house rent, conveyance and education, and a behaviorally 
determined level of other non-food expenses. For 2011-12, the Committee has estimated 
poverty ratio at all India level in rural areas as 30.9 per cent.
The Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011 was conducted to identify the 
multi dimensional nature of poverty. The focus of SECC 2011 is to arrive at the 
number of households with various deprivations. The concepts used in this Census 

Written Answers to [30 July, 2015]   Unstarred Questions 167
are different from those used by the Rangarajan Panel to arrive at poverty. The 
results from these two can be used for analyzing the different aspects of poverty 
in the country.The SECC methodology collected data on several parameters of 
rural households including criteria for automatic exclusion, automatic inclusion and 
deprivation. The SECC 2011 has not assessed 31.26 per cent rural Indians as poor.

by replacing the existing 2009 Policy; 
(b) if so, how the new one is different from the existing one;

required by industry?
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SKILL DEVELOPMENT 
AND ENTREPRENEURSHIP (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The 
new National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship 2015 is an attempt 
to provide a holistic and comprehensive roadmap for both job seekers as well as 
job creators by inclusion of specific sections on promotion of entrepreneurship. The 
Policy aims to bridge the skill gap by focusing on the key sectors that have the 
highest incremental human resource requirement viz. construction, retail and logistics. 
Strengthening Sector Skill Councils (SSCs), increasing industry linkages and creation of 
a national Labor Market Information System (LMIS) are efforts towards bridging the 
demand supply mismatch. A Quality Assurance framework embedded in National Skill 
Qualification Framework (NSQF) is envisaged to improve the consistency of outcomes

ISRO and NASA working on NISAR mission
1232. SHRI RANJIB BISWAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state:
(a) whether ISRO and NASA are jointly working on the NASA-ISRO Synthetic 
Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to codevelop and launch a dual frequency synthetic 
aperture radar satellite;
(b) if so, the details thereof along with the aims and objectives of the mission;
(c) the present status of the mission and the time by which the NISAR satellite 
is likely to be launched; and
(d) the total cost of the project and the expenditure sharing pattern between the 
two agencies?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER’S OFFICE  
(DR. JITENDRA SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir.  
(b) NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission is a dual frequency 
(L&S Band) Radar Imaging Satellite. In this joint mission, JPL/NASA will be 
responsible for design and development of L-band SAR, 12m unfurlable antenna, GPS 
system and data recorder. ISRO will be responsible for design and development of 
S-band SAR, Spacecraft Bus, Data Transmission System, Spacecraft integration and 
testing, launch using GSLV and on-orbit operations.
The aim and objectives of NISAR mission are:
 ● Design, Develop and launch a Dual frequency (L and S Band) Radar 
Imaging Satellite. 
 ● Explore newer application areas using L and S band microwave data, 
especially in natural resources mapping and monitoring; estimating agricultural 
biomass over full duration of crop cycle; assessing soil moisture; monitoring 
of floods and oil slicks; coastal erosion, coastline changes and variation 
of winds in coastal waters; assessment of mangroves; surface deformation 
studies due to seismic activities etc.
(c) Implementation Arrangement (IA), defining the roles and responsibilities of 
ISRO and NASA has been signed by the two agencies in September 2014. ISRO 
has completed the Baseline Design Reviews of Spacecraft and S-band SAR payload. 
JPL has successfully completed the Mission Concept and Key Decision Point reviews. 
The first Joint Steering Group (JSG) meeting of NISAR was held on July 21, 2015. 
NISAR satellite is expected to be launched during the year 2021.

INSAT type heavy communication satellites in geosynchronous orbits?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER’S OFFICE  
(DR. JITENDRA SINGH): (a) India has demonstrated the capability of launching 
1.4 ton class of satellites using Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and 2 ton 
class of satellites using Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) MK II 
to Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). 
(b) Indian Space Research Organisation has taken up the development of a 
new generation launch vehicle named GSLV MK III, with capability to launch up 
to 4 ton class of satellites to GTO. As a part of development, an experimental 
flight of GSLV MK III with passive cryogenic stage was successfully launched on 
18th December 2014 to validate the critical atmospheric regime of the flight. The 
endurance hot test of high thrust indigenous cryogenic engine of GSLV MK III 
has been successfully conducted for duration of 800 seconds on 16th July, 2015. 
After the successful qualification of the integrated cryogenic engine and stage, the 
first developmental flight of GSLV Mk III is planned.

1235. DR. K. P. RAMALINGAM: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is true that the ISRO would flight test an indigenously developed 
reusable satellite launch vehicle for the first time;
(b) whether it is also true that this is aimed at cutting down the costs of satellite 
launches to one-tenth the present rates; and 
(c) whether it is also true that at present the various stages in satellite launch 
vehicle fall of in succession during launch and cannot be reused making such launches 
expensive, if so, the details thereof?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER’S OFFICE  
(DR. JITENDRA SINGH): (a) Development of Reusable Launch Vehicles is a technical

first test flight (HEX-01) of Reusable Launch Vehicle–Technology Demonstrator

on the test flight results, further flights would be required to demonstrate reusability 
of the winged body.
(b) Reusable Launch Vehicles are aimed at cutting down the cost of satellite 
launches. However, the magnitude of cost reduction depends on the development and 
realization of fully reusable launch vehicle and its degree of reusability. 
(c) Yes, Sir. At present, operational launch vehicles in India are expendable 
launch vehicles, which are designed to be used only once and their stages are not

recovered for reuse. The launch vehicle typically consists of several rocket stages 
and the stages are jettisoned one by one during various phases of the mission as 
the launch vehicle gains desired altitude and speed.
Delay in GSLV launches and cryogenic engines
1236. DR. K. P. RAMALINGAM: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that long delay in realizing the indigenous GSLV launcher 
and its cryogenic engine had somewhat upset other project schedules;
(b) whether it is also true that another priority area was that of adding new 
facilities and improving the existing ones so that projects are completed in realistic 
time-frames;
(c) whether it is also true that the ISRO had started building the next generation 
launchers with double and triple the current GSLV capacity for putting satellites in 
space such as the GSLV and those powered by the futuristic semi cryogenic engine; 
and
(d) if so, the details thereof?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER’S OFFICE  
(DR. JITENDRA SINGH): (a) The delay in realizing the GSLV with indigenous 
cryogenic engine and stage had affected the launch schedules of 2 ton class of 
satellites to Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO).
(b) Yes, Sir. Action has been initiated to augment the facilities in the area of 
launch vehicle and satellites based on programmatic requirements.
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) ISRO is developing the GSLV MK III launch vehicle to launch up to 4 ton 
class of communication satellites to GTO. ISRO has also initiated the development 
of semi-cryogenic engine technology for use in future heavy lift launch vehicle 
configurations to achieve higher payload capability.
Projects pending for resolution
1237. SHRI DEVENDER GOUD T.: Will the Minister of STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that projects worth ` 18.47 lakh crores of 371 projects 
are pending for resolution before the Project Monitoring Group;
(b) if so, the details of pending project, project-wise and the reason for such 
pendency; and

190 Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions
(c) the efforts being made to clear the projects as early as possible?
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION [GENERAL (RETD.) V .K. SINGH]: (a) to (c) 
Project Monitoring Group (PMG) in Cabinet Secretariat has been facilitating resolution 
of issues of projects brought on the portal of PMG by the project proponents. Though 
no clearances are issued by PMG, it facilitates resolution of issues with Central and 
State Government agencies. The PMG has informed that as on 24th July 2015 there 
are 285 Projects still under consideration costing ` 12,27,499 crore and 30 Projects 
costing ` 1,06,552 crore are yet to be considered by the Sub-Groups. Thus in all 
315 Projects are under consideration/to be considered by the PMG. A list of these 
Projects is given in the Statement ( See below).
Issues uploaded by the project proponents on Project Monitoring Portal of Cabinet 
Secretariat, mainly relate to various clearances of Ministries including environment 
and forests, land acquisition and land related matters, financial issues, fuel and 
transportation issues etc. Some of the issues are structural or macroeconomic in 
nature, like lack of demand, equity availability etc.
Project Monitoring Group takes necessary action to resolve the issues raised on 
its portal. The issues in a project may relate to Central Ministries, State Governments 
or local authorities. Once projects/issues are accepted for consideration by the Project 
Monitoring Group, tripartite meetings are arranged involving the project proponents 
also. The decisions are taken by the authorities concerned in the light of relevant 
rules/regulations on the subject. PMG expedites resolution of the pending issues 
through constant monitoring and follow-up. With this objective, PMG has conducted 
337 meetings with Central Ministries and 112 meetings with State Governments so 
far. As a result, issues of 272 Projects with an investment of about ` 9,44,692 crore 
have been resolved.

Written Answers to [30 July, 2015]   Unstarred Questions 229
Expeditious implementation and completion of projects
1238. SHRI RANJIB BISWAL: Will the Minister of STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION be pleased to state:
(a) whether Government proposes to set up a three members dedicated group of 
eminent persons to recommend ways to kick start stalled projects vital to creating 
jobs and accelerating growth across farms and factories, if so, the details thereof;
(b) details of major projects which are facing delays for more than five years 
long with their original schedule of completion and the project cost;
(c) whether shortage of funds is major reason for these delays and if so, details 
thereof, project-wise; and
(d) details of bottlenecks identified and action taken to clear them to make way 
for expeditious implementation and completion of projects?
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION [GENERAL (RETD.) V .K. SINGH]: (a) No 
such proposal is under consideration.
(b) and (c) Government through the Ministry of Statistics and Programme 
Implementation monitors on-going Central Sector Infrastructure Projects costing ` 150 
crore and above on time and cost overruns, on the basis of information provided by 
the project implementing agencies. As on 01.06.2015 a total of 766 projects were on 
the monitor of this Ministry. Of these, 49 projects were showing time overruns of 
more than five years with respect to their original project implementation schedules. 
State-wise and Project-wise details of these 49 projects are given in the Statement-I 
(See below). of these, 6 projects have inter-alia reported shortage of funds as one of 
the reasons for delay. State-wise details of these 6 projects given in the Statement-II 
(See below).
(d) The major steps undertaken to ensure completion of Central Sector  
Infrastructure Projects without time and cost overruns include: rigorous project 
appraisal; On-line Computerized Monitoring System (OCMS) for better monitoring; 
setting up of Standing Committees in the Ministries for fixation of responsibility for 
time and cost overruns; regular review of infrastructure projects by the concerned 
administrative Ministries; and setting up of Central Sector Projects Coordination 
Committees (CSPCCs) in the States under the Chief Secretaries for removal of 
bottlenecks and for facilitating the speedy implementation of major projects.

Allocation of funds under AMRUT scheme
1240. DR. K. P. RAMALINGAM: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is true that under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban 
Transformation allocation of funds will be as per urban population and the number 
of cities and town in each State;
(b) whether it is also true that under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana in urban 
areas, the allocation will be based on the number of urban poor and slum dwellers; 
and 
(c) whether it is also true that new flagship programmes have mechanisms 
against delay, if so, the details thereof?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) Under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban 
Transformation (AMRUT), an equitable formula will be used to distribute the annual 
budgetary allocation in which equal (50:50) weightage is given to the urban population 
of each State/Union Territory (UT) (Census 2011) and the number of statutory towns 
in the State/UT. 
(b) Government of India has launched a new Mission ‘Housing for All’ (Urban) 
on 25.06.2015. As per scheme, Indicative State/ UT wise allocation will be made 
based on urban population and estimated slum population or other criteria as may 
be decided by Ministry. The allocation will be made separately for each component. 

Written Answers to [30 July, 2015]   Unstarred Questions 241
Ministry can change the inter-se allocation between different components with the 
approval of competent authority.
(c) AMRUT is a time bound programme to be implemented over a period of 5 
years from 2015 to 2020 with Reforms being completed in 4 years. The Ministry of 
Urban Development will only approve the State Annual Action Plan once in a year. 
The States/Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) will prepare, appraise and execute projects thus 
cutting down on time required for project completion. A further in-built mechanism to 
obviate delays is the stipulation that the State Government shall release the Central 
Assistance (CA) along with State share to the ULBs within seven working days of 
release of Central share. For period beyond seven days, the State shall be liable to 
pay interest. The Mission Guidelines provide for real-time monitoring at the State/ 
Urban Local Body (ULB) level and third party reviews.
The ‘Housing for All’ Mission scheme guidelines stipulates setting up of suitable 
monitoring mechanism at Central and State level for monitoring the progress of 
Mission and its different components. However, the timely implementation of the 
projects is the responsibility of the State/City Governments.

Waste treatement plants in country
1242. SHRI VIVEK GUPTA: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:
(a) the details of garbage and waste treatment plants functioning in the country, 
city and State-wise;
(b) whether all the garbage and waste treatment plants are functioning properly, 
if so, the details thereof and if not, the  reasons therefor along with the action taken/
being taken by Government in this regard;
(c) whether Government proposes to install new garbage and waste treatment 
plants and if so, the details thereof, city and State-wise; and 
(d) the time by which these plants are likely to be installed?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) and (b) As per the Report of the Task Force on 
Waste to Energy, published by NITI Aayog (erstwhile Planning Commission) in 
2014, only 22 States/UTs have set up waste processing and disposal facilities and 
the rest of the States/UTs have not setup till 2013. 279 Conventional composting, 
138 Vermi-composting, 172 Bio-methanation, 29 Refuse Derived Fuel (RDF) and 8 
Waste to Energy (W to E) plants are reported to have been established. Presently, 
many of the plants set up are either closed or under performing. The reason of this 
is diverse. However, most populist reasons public outcry, problems of marketing of 
compost, poor quality of feed stock, improper choice of technology and due to non-
availability of the right quantity and quality of wastes as was promised or envisaged 
etc. State-wise details of the waste processing and disposal facilities is given in the 
Statement ( See below).
(c) and (d)  Government of India has launched “Swachh Bharat Mission” (SBM) 
on 2nd October, 2014 with the target to make the country clean by 2nd October, 
2019. The Mission covers all 4041 statutory towns/cities as per 2011 Census. One 
of the admissible components under SBM is Solid Waste Management with Central 
support up to 20% of the project cost in the form of Viability Gap Funding 
(VGF)/Grant. The remaining funds have to be generated through private sector 
participation/State Government/ULB contribution. Under SBM, ULBs can adopt all 
feasible waste processing methods for efficient management of solid waste, as per 
the local conditions.

Regional Plan 2021
1246. SHRI DIGVIJAYA SINGH: Will the Minster of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:
(a) what action has been taken by the Board and Government to ensure that the 
development in the National Capital Region (NCR) is as per the published Regional 
Plan; 
(b) whether the Board or Central Government found violation of Regional Plan 
and the NCR Planning Board Act, 1985 by the State and the Board; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) National Capital Region Planning Board (NCRPB) 
has informed that the implementation of the broad policies and proposals of the 
Regional Plan are to be ensured by the participating States as per the respective 
Sub-Regional Plans (SRPs) which are required to be in conformity with the Regional 
Plan (RP). Further, National Capital Region (NCR) Planning and Monitoring Cells 
were created in all the NCR participating States, which are under the administrative 
control of the respective State Governments, for monitoring of implementation of 
Regional Plan, among other tasks. The NCR Planning and Monitoring Cells have 

248 Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions
also been assigned the specific task to bring to the notice of the Board any case 
of violation of the Regional Plan.
(b) NCRPB has informed that no case of violation has been reported by any

(c) NCRPB has informed that any development in the region including National 
Capital Territory (NCT-Delhi), which is one of the sub-regions of NCR, has to be

Problems related to rapid urbanisation
1248. SHRI AAYANUR MANJUNATHA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether different parts of the country have experienced rapid urbanisation 
putting pressure on existing infrastructure ;

Written Answers to [30 July, 2015]   Unstarred Questions 249
(b) if so, the details thereof along with steps taken by Government for sprucing 
up infrastructure in recently urbanised parts of the country during the last three years, 
State-wise;
(c) whether increasing pollution, slums, traffic snarls, etc., have become major concerns 
in urban areas, if so, the details of schemes launched to tackle the problem; and
(d) the details of the schemes sanctioned and work started under these schemes 
in various States during the last three years, State-wise?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) Yes, Sir. According to the High Powered Expert 
Committee (HPEC) Report on Urban Infrastructure and Services, States such as Tamil 
Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh 
have experienced rapid urbanisation.
(b) The Jawaharlal Nehru Urban Renewal Mission (JnNURM) was a Mission to 
spruce up infrastructure. During the last three details of projects taken up are given 
in the Statement ( See below).
(c) and (d) The steps taken by Central Government to tackle traffic issues, 
pollution etc. in the past three years are given below:
(i) To encourage a shift from private mode of transport to public transport 
inorder to check the alarming increase of private vehicles, the Central 
Government is popularising the public transport and emphasizing to provide 
quick, comfortable, reliable, safe and affordable public transport as envisaged 
in the National Urban Transport Policy, 2006. Accordingly, the Central 
Government is supporting various public transport projects such as Metro 
Rail, Bus Rapid Transport System (BRTS) and modern city bus services as 
per urban bus specifications in various cities in India. During the last three 
years the Central Government has sanctioned metro rail projects in the cities 
of Mumbai, Jaipur, Bangalore, Nagpur and Ahmedabad to provide safe, 
affordable, reliable and sustainable access to transportation to the rapidly 
growing urban population.
(ii) The Ministry of Urban Development has also approved 22 BRTS projects in 
12 cities, out of which, 7 projects have been completed and the remaining 
projects are at different stages of implementation. Total 15484 buses 
were sanctioned to 61 cities during 2009-10. Further, Ministry of Urban 
Development sanctioned 12000 buses (funding restricted to 10000 buses 
only, 2000 buses sanctioned as a cushion) to 142 cities/cluster of cities in 
22 States in the year 2013-14 under JnNURM.

250 Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions
(iii) To ease out the traffic congestion in various States of the Country, an 
Advisory has been issued to all the States and UTs regarding identifying 
the most congested areas in their cities, getting a proper study done on 
various aspects of congestion of traffic as per city requirement and consider 
adopting ‘Congestion Charges’ as a measure to decongest a particular area 
such as Central Business District, increasing mode share of cycling as well 
as public transport and mobility of the people besides controlling pollution.
(iv) Further, to promote cleaner and greener environment, the Ministry has 
initiated the Sustainable Urban Transport Project (SUTP) with the support 
of the World Bank, Global Environment Facility (GEF) and the UNDP. The 
project aims to promote environmentally sustainable urban transport in India 
and to improve environment-friendly transport modes through demonstration 
projects in select cities.

Encroachment on DDA land in Bindapur
1249. SHRI PRAMOD TIWARI: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether  it is a fact that there is  encroachment  on Mixed Land Use 
(MLU) plots, flats, central park, small parks and vacant/unused land belonging to 
DDA in DDA flats Bindapur, Pocket-3, New Delhi;
(b) whether it is a fact that many MLU plots and flats are still to be allotted;
(c) whether it is a fact that proper upkeep of DDA properties is not being 
maintained; and
(d) whether it is also a fact that water bill has not been paid by many flat 
owners to DDA, if so, what action Government proposes to take and the details 
thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) Delhi Development Authority (DDA) has informed 
that one mazar and one small temple exist on the Mixed Land Use (MLU) plot in 
Bindapur, Pocket-3, New Delhi. There is no encroachment in DDA flats at Bindapur 
Pocket-3, New Delhi.
(b) There are some MLU plots, which are to be auctioned to the highest bidder. 
There is no MLU flat in Bindapur Pocket-3, New Delhi.
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) In case of non-payment of water bills by the flat owners, DDA recovers 
the amount by adding the outstanding amount with late fee in the next bill.
Panaji as smart city
1250. SHRI SHANTARAM NAIK: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:
(a) whether city of Panaji in Goa has been included in the cities to be developed 
as smart cities in the country, if so, when was the decision taken;
(b) facilities proposed to be provided for the city under the scheme and the 
amount proposed to be spent;
(c) whether Municipal Corporation of Panaji City has been taken on board, 
and any discussion preliminary or otherwise have been held with the corporation; 
and

278 Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions
(d) any plan for the smart city of Panaji has been drawn, the details 
thereof?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) to (d) The “Smart Cities Mission” for development 
of 100 smart cities was launched on 25th June, 2015. The Mission Statement and 
Guidelines were also released during the event and are available on Ministry’s website 
(moud.gov.in). The selection of Smart Cities follows a Challenge (Competition) 
process. In the Stage-1 of the Competition, the States including Goa, have to shortlist 
cities based on the criteria given in the Guidelines. Thereafter, the shortlisted cities 
have to compete in Stage-2 of the contest in which Smart City Proposal has to 
be prepared.
Assistance to States for Swachh Bharat Mission
1251. DR. R. LAKSHMANAN: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:
(a) details of the ways and means in which Government is supporting the efforts 
taken by the State Government under Swachh Bharat Mission; and 
(b) details of autonomy/power devolved to Urban Local Bodies (ULB) under 
this Mission?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) and (b) The estimated cost of implementation of 
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) (Urban) for its various components is ` 62,009 
crore. The Government of India share as per approved funding pattern amounts 
to ` 14,623 crore. For individual household toilets, the Centre is providing an 
incentive of ` 4000 per household toilet and for community toilets the incentive is 
in the form of 40% Viability Gap Funding (VGF)/Grant. In the case of Solid Waste 
Management the Centre is providing 20% VGF/Grant for each project. 15% of the 
Central allocation is allotted to the States for Public Awareness, Information, Education 
and Communication (IEC) activities, Capacity Building (CB) and Administrative and 
Office Expenses (A&OE).
So far, ` 1010.09 crore has been disbursed to the States as Central Share. 
While actual devolution of power and autonomy given to the ULBs for the 
Mission are within the purview of the State Governments, however the guidelines 
of the Mission ensure that the ULBs have a vital role to play in achieving the 
targets/objectives.

CEO for smart cities
1252. SHRI RITABRATA BANERJEE: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state whether Government is planning to appoint 
Chief Executive Officers for smart cities, if so, the details thereof?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): The Smart Cities Mission was launched on 25th June, 
2015 and the Guidelines were also released on the occasion which is available on 
the Ministry’s website ( moud.gov.in). The implementation of the Mission at the City 
level will be done by a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) created for the purpose. 
Each smart city will have a SPV which will be headed by a full time CEO. The 
functions of the CEO include:
(i) Overseeing and managing the general conduct of the day-to-day operations 
of the SPV subject to the supervision and control of the Board. 
(ii) Entering into contracts or arrangements for and on behalf of the Company 
in all matters within the ordinary course of the Company’s business.
(iii) To formulate and submit to the Board of Directors for approval a Human 
Resource Policy that will lay down procedures for creation of staff positions, 
qualifications of staff, recruitment procedures, compensation and termination 
procedures.
(iv) Recruitment and removal of the senior management of the Company and 
the creation of new positions in accordance with the Company’s approved 
budget and the recruitment or increase of employees in accordance with the 
Human Resource Policy laid down by the Board.
(v) Supervising the work of all employees and managers of the Company and 
the determination of their duties, responsibilities and authority. 
Mono-Metro Rail in Chennai
1253. DR. E. M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Mono-Metro Railway Scheme in Chennai is going to be further 
developed by Central Government participation; and  
(b) if so, the terms and conditions of participation of Government and the State 
Government of Tamil Nadu from the original MoU and the monetary commitment, 
year-wise and revenue sharing?

280 Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) and (b) Urban Transport is intertwined with urban 
development, which is a State subject and hence, Mono-Metro Rail Projects are 
initiated/proposed by the State Governments. The proposals of Mono-Metro Rail 
Projects received from the State Governments are considered by Government of India 
(GoI) under the ambit of National Urban Transport Policy (NUTP), 2006. 
The terms and conditions of participation of GoI for further development of 
Mono-Metro Railway Scheme in Chennai will be as per the NUTP, 2006 and could 
be considered only after such proposals alongwith Detailed Project Report containing 
the financing pattern, if any, is received.
Cities covered under smart city project
1254. SHRI BHUPINDER SINGH: Will the Minister of URBAN  DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:
(a) in how many years the Ministry will be able to cover development of  500 
cities in the country;
(b) whether it is a fact that the Ministry has planned to cover only 100 (one 
hundred) smart cities in three phases as under, first year 20, second year 40 and 
third year 40 cities; and
(c) how much Government will spent on each smart cities, year-wise details 
thereof?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI BABUL SUPRIYO): (a) The Government of India has launched a new Mission 
“Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT)” on 25.06.2015 
with the objective to develop basic urban infrastructure in the 500 cities/towns. The 
Mission has started in 2015-16 and is initially planned up to 2019-20.
(b) Yes Sir, in the Smart Cities Mission.
(c) The Smart Cities Mission was launched on 25th June, 2015. The Mission 
Statement and Guidelines were also released which are available on Ministry’s website 
(moud.gov.in). This Mission will be operated as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) 
and the Central Government proposes to give financial support to the Mission to the 
extent of ` 48,000 crores over five years i.e. an average ` 200 crores in the first 
year followed by ` 100 crore every year for the next three years for every smart 
city which is finally selected.

Private food manufacturers in ICDS 
1259. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that some State Governments are giving contracts to 
private food manufacturers to supply nutritious food for vulnerable infants and 
pregnant women and nursing mothers under the Supplementary Nutrition Programme 
of Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS), despite Supreme Court order 
prohibiting private players in the ICDS Scheme; and
(b) if so, the States which have given contracts to private players and 
Government’s reaction thereto?
THE MINISTER OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI  
MANEKA SANJAY GANDHI): (a) and (b) The Integrated Child Development Services 
(ICDS) Scheme is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme implemented by States/UTs. The 
Scheme provides for a package of six services including Supplementary Nutrition 
(SNP) for children in the age group of 0-6 years and pregnant and lactating mothers.
The Supreme Court vide their order dated 07.10.2004, in a Public Interest 
Litigation – W.P. No.196 of 2001, had directed that the contractors shall not be used 
for supply of nutrition in Aanganwadis and preferably ICDS funds shall be spent 
by making use of village communities, self-help groups and Mahila Mandals for 
buying of grains and preparation of meals. These directions were reiterated by the 
Supreme Court on 13.12.2006 and 22.04.2009. Accordingly, all the States/UTs were 
addressed on 17.12.2004 for compliance of Supreme Court order dated 07.10.2004. 
Later on, in Civil Appeal No.7104 of 2011–Shagun Mahila Udyogik Sahakari 
Sanstha Maradit versus State of Maharashtra and others the Supreme Court gave 
judgement dated 19th August, 2011. All the States/UTs were requested on 9th May, 
2012 to comply with the directions of the Supreme Court in the aforesaid judgement.

Reforms in procedure of adoption
1263. SHRIMATI GUNDU SUDHARANI: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) the domestic and international procedures being followed in adoption;
(b) whether it is true that Government is planning to bring in reforms in the 
adoption procedures; and
(c) if so, the details thereon and the reasons therefor?
THE MINISTER OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT   
(SHRIMATI MANEKA SANJAY GANDHI): (a) For in-country domestic adoption, 
Prospective Adoptive Parents (PAPs) register with a Specialised Adoption Agency 
(SAA) or online in the Child Adoption Resource Information and Guidance System 
(CARINGS). After completing the Home Study Report (HSR) of the PAPs, the 
Specialised Adoption Agency matches a suitable child with them. On receipt of the 
acceptance by the PAPs, the child is given in pre-adoption foster care to them by 
the agency. Thereafter, the adoption order is obtained by the SAA in favour of the 
adoption of the child.
For inter-country adoption, the PAPs living abroad register with an Authorized 
Foreign Adoption Agency (AFAA) in the country of their residence. The AFAA, 
after completing the HSR and other required documentation regarding the PAPs, 
register such PAPs in the CARINGS. The PAPs found eligible after initial screening 
by the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) are referred to a Recognized 
Indian Placement Agency (RIPA). The RIPA then refers a suitable child to the PAPs 
along with child study report and medical examination report through the concerned 
AFAA.  On the receipt of the acceptance of the referred child by the PAPs, required 
documents in original from the AFAA, the RIPA obtains the No-Objection Certificate 
(NOC) from CARA and files an application in the concerned Court on behalf of 
the PAPs for an order in favour of such adoption. On the receipt of the adoption 

Written Answers to [30 July, 2015]   Unstarred Questions 295
Order from the Court, the RIPA obtains the passport for the child and intimates 
the PAPs to come to India for taking the child to their country of residence. The 
PAPs visit the agency to collect the child after obtaining visa/travel document from 
the diplomatic mission of the country of their residence. The PAPs can also take 
the child in pre-adoption foster care in India, pending the adoption order from the 
Court, but after the issuance of NOC by CARA.
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The Government has notified Guidelines Governing Adoption 
of Children-2015 on 17.07.2015 to be effective from 01.08.2015. To further simplify 
the procedure and to minimize delay in the process of adoption, some of the key 
changes contemplated in the existing guidelines are provisions for linking the orphan/ 
abandoned/surrendered children of all Child Care Institutions (CCIs) to the adoption 
system, making the entire adoption process online, treating NRI prospective adoptive 
parents at par with the domestic prospective adoptive parents, reducing the timeframe 
for completion of Home study report from two months to one month, All Specialised 
Adoption Agencies (SAA) would be authorised to do in-country and inter-country 
adoption.  This will enable the special needs and older children in such agencies 
(who rarely go in domestic adoptions) to find suitable family through inter-country 
adoption.
Malnourishment in children
1264. SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) the total number of districts with high extent of malnourishment in children, 
State-wise;
(b) whether Government has formulated any scheme to increase dietary intake 
of severely malnourished children in the affected districts, if so, the details thereof; 
and 
(c) the follow up action taken by Government in this regard?
THE MINISTER OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRIMATI MANEKA SANJAY GANDHI): (a) A total of 200 districts with high 
extent of malnourishment in children have been identified under the Integrated 
Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme of the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development. The list of 200 high-burden districts are given in the Statement  
(See below).
(b) and (c) Under the ICDS Scheme, supplementary nutrition is provided to 
bridge the gap between the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) and Average 

296 Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions
Dietary Intake (ADI). Severely malnourished children below 6 years of age are 
provided nutritious food in the form of (i) Hot Cooked Meal, (ii) Morning Snack 
and (iii) Micronutrient Fortified Food and/or Energy-dense Food as Take Home 
Ration (THR) as per nutritional norms that is additional 300 calories of energy and  
8-10 g of protein (in addition to 500 calories of energy and 12-15 g of protein 
provided to the children below 6 years of age).
Additionally, under the ICDS Scheme, the Government has rolled out a Community 
based management programme, “Sneha Shivir”, for moderate and severely malnourished 
children under 6 years across the country. Sneha Shivir has been introduced in 200 
high burden districts of the country and is serviced through an Additional Anganwadi 
Worker/ Nutrition Counselor at the Anganwadi Centre.
The scheme provides for holding of Sneha Shivirs at an Anganwadi Centre 
(AWC) selected from amongst a cluster of 4-5 AWCs in areas where the number of 
moderately and severely underweight children is high. Its overall goal is to ensure 
quick rehabilitation of undernourished children; enable families to sustain rehabilitation; 
and prevent future undernutrition by changing behaviors in child care, feeding and 
health seeking.

1275. SHRI D. BANDYOPADHYAY: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether Government is aware that an estimate from the 2011 Census 
reveals that the child sex ratio of boys to girls, 0-6 years, is at its highest level 
since Independence and these missing women are distributed across the country 

Written Answers to [30 July, 2015]   Unstarred Questions 311
with Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab showing very high mortality compared 
to female population; and
(b) if so, whether Government is contemplating any special measures to contain 
and reduce the number of “Missing Women” in those States?
THE MINISTER OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRIMATI MANEKA SANJAY GANDHI): (a) Yes, As per Census 2011 data, Child 
Sex Ratio (CSR) stands at 918 girls per 1000 boys in the age group of 0-6 years, 
much lower than the figure of 927 in 2001 Census. As per Census 2011, 15 States 
are below or equal to national average of 918 including Haryana, Madhya Pradesh 
and Punjab. 429 districts spread across 33 States (including Telanagana) have shown 
decline in CSR from 2001 to 2011. The CSR in States of Haryana, Madhya Pradesh 
and Punjab is as follows:  
Haryana: As per the Census 2011 the Child Sex Ratio in the State of Haryana 
is 834 which is well below the national average of 918. 
Punjab: As per the Census 2011 the Child Sex Ratio in the State of Punjab is 
846 which is also lower than the national average of 918. 
Madhya Pradesh:  Madhya Pradesh recorded a 14 point decline in CSR from 
932 girls per 1000 boys in 2001 to 918 in 2011. 
(b) Addressing declining Child Sex Ratio is a priority of the Government. Beti 
Bachao, Beti Padhao (BBBP) Scheme has been launched by the Prime Minister on 
22nd January, 2015 in Panipat, Haryana. BBBP addresses the declining Child Sex Ratio 
(CSR) and related issues of disempowerment of women over a life-cycle continuum. 
It is a tri-ministerial initiative of Ministries of Women and Child Development, Health 
and Family Welfare and Human Resource Development.This Scheme focusses on 
awareness and advocacy campaign at national level, enforcement of Pre-Conception 
and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PC&PNDT) Act and multi-sectoral action in 
select 100 districts (low on CSR) in the first phase. 
Out of these selected districts, 12 districts from Haryana, 11 district from Punjab 
and 4 districts from Madhya Pradesh have been identified for focussed attention.

of the mother to look after the normal health and nutritional needs of the child 
through proper nutrition and health education.

Irregularities under PMGSY
†*63. SHRI RAMDAS ATHAWALE: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT  
be pleased to state:
(a) whether Government is aware of any irregularities committed under the 
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) during the last three years and if so, 
the details thereof; and 
(b) whether Government has conducted any inquiry in this regard and if so, the 
details and the outcome thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHAUDHARY BIRENDER 
SINGH): (a) and (b) 'Rural Roads' is a State subject and Pradhan Mantri Gram 
Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) is a one-time special intervention of Central Government 
to improve the rural infrastructure through construction of roads. 
In order to bring the execution of PMGSY works to the desired quality standard, 
a three tier quality management mechanism has been institutionalized. Under the 
first tier, the Programme Implementation Units (PIUs) are required to ensure process 
control through mandatory tests on material and workmanship at field laboratory. 
The second tier is a structured independent quality monitoring at the State level 
through State Quality Monitors (SQMs) to ensure that every work is inspected at 
initial stage, middle stage and final stage of the construction. Under the third tier, 
independent National Quality Monitors (NQMs) are deployed for random inspection 
of road works to monitor quality and also to provide guidance of senior professionals 
to the field functionaries. Based on the periodic monitoring of quality of roads 
under the 3-tier mechanism, corrective measures, wherever necessary, are taken by 
the State Governments.
As per the PMGSY Programme Guidelines, ensuring quality of road works under 
PMGSY is the responsibility of State Rural Roads Development Agency (SRRDA), 
which is the Implementing Agency in the States. All such complaints are, therefore, 
referred to the State Quality Coordinators of respective SRRDA for taking necessary 
corrective action and furnishing action taken report. In case adequate response is not 
received within the prescribed time schedule, the National Rural Roads Development 
Agency (NRRDA) deputes National Quality Monitor (NQM) for enquiry, and based 
on the report of the NQM, further action is taken. 
During the year 2012-13, 2013-14, 2014-15 and 2015-16 (upto to June, 2015) 
170 such cases have been received in National Rural Roads Development Agency

being imparted in the minority educational institutions under the Right of Children

*65. SHRI D. KUPENDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES,

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES, RIVER DEVELOPMENT AND 
GANGA REJUVENATION (SUSHRI UMA BHARTI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Cleaning 
of river Ganga was initiated in 1985 under Ganga Action Plan-I (GAP-I) and further it 
was continued since 1993 as Ganga Action Plan-II (GAP-II). The National Ganga River 
Basin Authority (NGRBA) was launched in 2009 with the renewed vision of cleaning

river Ganga using a basin wide approach. National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG)

of National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA). The Union Cabinet has approved

Construction of roads under PMGSY 
†*70. DR. SATYANARAYAN JATIYA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the latest status of constructed and unconstructed roads under the Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) relating to connected and unconnected villages, 
along with their length, State-wise; and 
(b) the steps taken for improvement and maintenance of present PMGSY roads 
and the details of funds provided to the States during the last five years, year-wise 
and State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHAUDHARY BIRENDER 
SINGH): (a) Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme with the objective to provide single all-weather road connectivity to all eligible 
unconnected habitations, existing in the core network, in rural areas of country. The 
programme envisages connecting all eligible unconnected habitations with a population 
of 500 persons and above (as per 2001 Census) in plain areas and 250 persons 
and above (as per 2001 Census) in Special Category States (Arunachal Pradesh, 
Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura Himachal Pradesh, 
Jammu and Kashmir and Uttarakhand), Tribal (Schedule-V) Areas, the Desert Areas  
(as identified in Desert Development Programme) and in Selected Tribal and Backward 
Districts (as identified by the Ministry of Home Affairs/Planning Commission). The 
PMGSY permits upgradation (to prescribed standards) of existing rural roads in 
districts where all the eligible habitations of the designated population size have been 
provided all weather road connectivity. For most intensive IAP blocks, as identified 
by the Ministry of Home Affairs the unconnected habitations with population 100 
and above (as per 2001 Census) are eligible to be covered under PMGSY . Under 
PMGSY , the unit of programme is a habitation and not a revenue village. State-wise 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

338 Written Ans. to Std. and [RAJYA SABHA] Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015
details of number and length of road works sanctioned and completed (as reported 
by various States upto June, 2015) are given in the Statement ( See below).
(b) All PMGSY roads are covered by a 5-year maintenance contract, entered 
into along with construction contract, with the same contractor, in accordance with 
the Standard Bidding Document (SBD). Maintenance funds to service the contract are 
budgeted by the State Governments. On expiry of 5-year post-construction maintenance, 
the State Governments are required to make necessary budget provision to place such 
roads under zonal maintenance contracts. Accordingly, no Central funds are released 
to the States for maintenance of PMGSY roads.
In order to bring the execution of PMGSY works to the desired quality standard, 
a three tier quality management mechanism has been institutionalized. Under the 
first tier, the Programme Implementation Units (PIUs) are required to ensure process 
control through mandatory tests on material and workmanship at field laboratory. 
The second tier is a structured independent quality monitoring at the State level 
through State Quality Monitors (SQMs) to ensure that every work is inspected at 
initial stage, middle stage and final stage of the construction. Under the third tier, 
independent National Quality Monitors (NQMs) are deployed for random sample 
inspection of road works to monitor quality and also to provide guidance of senior 
professionals to the field functionaries. Based on the periodic monitoring of quality 
of roads under the 3-tier mechanism, corrective measures, wherever necessary, are 
taken by the State Governments.
National Rural Roads Development Agency (NRRDA) in partnership with 
International Labour Organization (ILO) and World Bank has extended support to the 
States in the maintenance management of rural roads. Accordingly, a Model Policy 
Framework for Maintenance of Rural Roads along with a Guidance note finalized in 
close consultation with the States has been shared with all States. Based on these 
documents, the States have been advised to formulate their Rural Road Maintenance 
Policies to suit State specific needs.
PMGSY-II, launched in May, 2013, envisages consolidation of the existing Rural 
Road Network to improve its overall efficiency as a provider of transportation services 
for people, goods and services. It aims to cover upgradation of existing selected 
rural roads based on their economic potential and their role in facilitating the growth 
of rural market centres and rural hubs. During the Twelfth five year plan period, 
Upgradation of 50,000 km road length at an estimated cost of ` 33,030 crore (at 
2012-13 prices) has been approved by the Union Cabinet. At present, 7 States (Andhra 
Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh) 
have been sanctioned road works under P MGSY-II covering 11,234 Km road length.

Changes in education system
*73. SHRI PRAMOD TIWARI: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the present education system in the country is not 
in consonance with the present day needs of the country;  
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; 
(c) whether comprehensive changes in this education system are needed; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government thereto and the steps Government has 
taken so far in this regard?
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRIMATI SMRITI ZUBIN IRANI): (a) to (d) The National Policy on Education 
(NPE), 1986, which  was modified  in 1992, envisages, inter-alia, a National System of 
Education to bring about uniformity in education, making adult education programmes 
a mass movement, providing universal access, ensuring retention and improving quality 
in elementary education, special emphasis on education of girls, establishment of pace-
setting schools, like Navodaya Vidyalayas in each district, vocationalisation of secondary 

342 Written Ans. to Std. and [RAJYA SABHA] Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015
education, synthesis of knowledge and inter-disciplinary research in higher education, 
starting more Open Universities in the States, strengthening of the All India Council 
for Technical Education, encouraging sports, physical education, Yoga and adoption 
of an effective evaluation method. Since the last Policy, several changes have taken 
place which call for a revision of the Policy. For this purpose, the Government of 
India has initiated the consultation process of formulating a New Education Policy 
(NEP) to meet the changing dynamics of the population’s requirement with regard 
to quality education, innovation and research, aiming to make India a knowledge 
superpower by equipping its students with the necessary skills and knowledge and to 
eliminate the shortage of manpower in science, technology, academics and industry. A 
multiple level consultative processes involving all stakeholders, such as, educationists, 
teachers, and students across all levels are envisaged. The online consultation process 
has already been launched on www.MyGov.in portal on 26.01.2015 and nearly 21,500 
suggestions have already been received on 33 identified themes. The grass roots 
level consultation from the Gram Panchayat level through the Block and District to 
State level has started. The Government has set a time frame to formulate the New 
Education Policy by December, 2015. A High Level meeting was taken by Minister 
for Human Resource Development on 14.02.2015 to discuss the consultative process 
for formulation of NEP and invite suggestions of other Government of India Ministries 
and Departments to devise curriculum from their perspective. Another meeting was 
also taken by the Minister on 21st March, 2015 with the State Education Ministers 
and Secretaries of School Education and Higher Education Departments regarding 
outlining the consultation process. The NEP Task Force has been set up to monitor 
the progress of the consultation process from time to time.  All relevant documents 
related to New Education Policy can be accessed from NEP corner on MHRD 
website www.mhrd.gov.in.

Reservation against reverse bidding mechanism for coal blocks
651. DR. T. N. SEEMA: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state:
(a) whether a lot of companies have approached Government expressing 
reservations regarding the reverse bidding mechanism and raised a lot of queries 
regarding the same;
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons for opting the reverse bidding 
mechanism; 
(c) whether such a step by Government is just to favour select large business 
houses as the medium size companies would have disadvantages against large 
companies in terms of sustainability due to this mechanism;
(d) if so, the details thereof; and
(e) if not, the reasons therefor?
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRI PIYUSH  
GOYAL): (a) to (e) Some reservations were expressed by a few stakeholders regarding 
reverse bidding methodology; however,  reverse bidding methodology was adopted in 
the auction of coal mines earmarked for power sector under the provisions of Coal 
Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 and the rules framed thereunder in order to 
ensure that there is no rise in power tariffs. Under the reverse bidding methodology, 
bidders have to submit bids below the Coal India Limited’s notified price for 
corresponding grade of coal which is the ceiling price. The lowest bid submitted is 

Written Ans. to Std. and [30 July, 2015]   Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015 357
taken as the fuel cost in determination of power tariff. In case, bid price reaches  
` Zero in reverse bidding, the bidding changes to a forward one where bidders have 
to quote additional premium payable to the State Government where the mine is 
located, over and above the fixed reserve price of ` 100/- per tonne. The reverse 
bidding methodology for auction of Coal mines for power sector has been designed 
keeping in view the interest of power consumers. Hon’ble High Court of Delhi in a 
judgement has also observed that the process of electronic auction does not appear 
to be arbitrary or irrational and the auction process is not designed to favour any 
particular bidder.
New auction methodology
652. SHRI DEREK O'BRIEN: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that Government is considering a new auction methodology, 
where a bidder would be required to quote separate figures for fixed charges and 
variable charges;
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the current laws and auction methodology are perfect; and
(d) if not, what are Government's plans on these?
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF Coal (SHRI PIYUSH 
GOYAL): (a) and (b) There is no such proposal under consideration.
(c) and (d) The objectives of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015, the 
Rules made thereunder and the auction methodology are to put in place a regime for 
allocation of coal mines in a transparent and objective manner. Hon’ble High Court 
of Delhi has also observed in a judgement that the process of electronic auction 
does not appear to be arbitrary or irrational and the auction process is not designed 
to favour any particular bidder.
In the third tranche of auction, auction design has been slightly modified in 
order to prevent the possibility of cartelization/price manipulation whereby multiple 
bids submitted by a Company or a Group in Initial Price Offer (IPO) for a coal 
mine would be counted as one for the purpose of determining the eligibility to 
participate in final price offer (FPO). This provision would also increase number of 
bidders in Final Price Offer in case a single company submits multiple bids thereby 
engendering more competition.
As there is always a scope for improvement, necessary changes shall be 
incorporated as and when any shortcomings are noticed in the auction design.

Per capita availability of drinking water in rural areas
660. SHRI PARIMAL NATHWANI: Will the Minister of DRINKING WATER 
AND SANITATION be pleased to state:
(a) whether the households living in the rural areas are getting 40 litres of 
water per capita per day (1pcd) as stipulated under the guidelines of the National 
Rural Drinking Water Programme;
(b) if so, the details thereof; and
(c) if not, the measures taken by Government to ensure availability of requisite 
quantity of water in the rural areas within a definite time-frame?

368 Written Ans. to Std. and [RAJYA SABHA] Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF DRINKING WATER 
AND SANITATION (SHRI RAM KRIPAL YADA V): (a) and (b) Under the National 
Rural Drinking Water Programme (NRDWP) the norm for providing drinking water 
to the rural population in the country is 40 litres per capita per day (lpcd) . As on 
1.4.2015, 74.14% of rural population has been fully covered with the availability of 
minimum 40 litres per capita per day (lpcd). The balance 21.96% of the population 
are partially covered and are getting drinking water supply less than the  required 
norms. Moreover, 3.90% of the population are not getting potable drinking water due 
to various contaminants like arsenic, fluoride, iron, nitrate and salinity.
As per the data entered by the States on the Integrated Management Information 
System (IMIS) of the Ministry as on 1.4.2015 out of a total of 17,13,303 rural 
habitations in the country there are 12,70,199 fully covered, 3,76,343 partially covered 
and 66,761 quality affected habitations in the country.
(c) Drinking Water supply is a State subject. Government of India supplements 
the efforts of the State Governments with technical and financial assistance for 
provision of safe drinking water supply in the rural areas of the country under 
the Centrally sponsored National Rural Drinking Water Programme (NRDWP). The 
State Governments are vested with powers to select, plan, approve and implement 
Drinking Water Supply Schemes under the NRDWP, to cover more habitations with 
piped drinking water supply. 
Government has made a Strategic Plan for providing drinking water supply in 
rural areas of the country. Under the Strategic Plan for rural drinking water Supply 
for the period 2011-2022, covering the two Five Year Plan periods, the interim 
goal till 2017 i.e. by the end of Twelfth Five Year Plan period, is to cover 50% 
of all rural households with piped water supply, and 35% of rural households with 
household tap connections. By 2022, the goal is to cover 90% of rural households 
with piped water supply and with 80% having household tap connections.

Written Ans. to Std. and [30 July, 2015]   Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015 377
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF DRINKING WATER AND

Water and Sanitation, Government of India has advised all States including Bihar to 
provide safe drinking water in adequate quantity through piped water supply Schemes 
from safe drinking water sources, preferably surface water sources, in a phased manner 
to all rural habitations in the country. To achieve this goal, the Government’s work 
plan is to ensure that at least 50% of rural households are provided with piped water 
Supply; at least 35% of rural households have piped water Supply with a household 
connection by 2017. Further, by 2022, to ensure that at least 90% of rural households

share funds under the Centrally sponsored National Rural Drinking Water Programme.

of 3-5 years, and that rural population cannot be put to risk of consuming unsafe 
drinking water, till such time, the Government of India had suggested all States 
including Bihar to set up community water purification plants to provide 8-10 litres 
per capita per day of safe drinking water for drinking and cooking purposes in 
water quality affected habitations with high priority to arsenic and fluoride affected 
habitations. As informed by States, they have started installation of Community based 
Reverse Osmosis Plants in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Punjab, 
Kerala, Puducherry, Haryana, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and few plants in

areas of the country. Under the Strategic Plan for the period 2011-2022, covering

Supply, and 35% of rural households with household tap connections. By 2022, the 
goal is to cover 90% of rural households with piped water Supply and with 80% 
having household tap connections.

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SMRITI 
ZUBIN IRANI): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Certain complaints for alleged irregularities,

671. SHRI A VINASH PANDE: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Central Government is aware that the State Government of 
Maharashtra has decided to treat children going to madarsas as not enrolled in any

out-of-school children; 
(b) whether Government approves of such a classification of children attending 
madarsas; 

384 Written Ans. to Std. and [RAJYA SABHA] Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015
(c) whether this is permissible in accordance with the constitutional right of 
minorities to set up their own educational institutions; and 
(d) if not, whether Government has taken any steps to restrain the State 
Government of Maharashtra from implementing such an illegal classification through 
its survey?
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SMRITI 
ZUBIN IRANI): (a) to (d) State Government of Maharashtra has informed that 
a survey of out of school children across the State was conducted on 4th July, 
2015. The State Government has further reported that as per the Right to Free 
and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 every child of the age 6-14 should be 
enrolled in a school and that a school must give education to students according to 
syllabus prepared by the Academic Authority declared by the Government. The State 
Government has also stated that education in any school which is not teaching as 
per the curriculum prepared by the Academic Authority of the State ( i.e. Maharashtra 
State Council for Educational Research and Training, Pune) is considered as informal 
education, therefore children enrolled in those schools should be treated as Out of 
School Children. 
Section 2(n) of the RTE Act, 2009 defines a ‘school’ as any recognized school 
imparting elementary education and includes-
(i) a school established, owned or controlled by the appropriate Government or 
a local authority;
(ii) an aided school receiving aid or grant to meet whole or part of its expenses 
from the appropriate Government or the local authority;
(iii) a school belonging to specified category; and 
(iv) an unaided school not receiving any kind of aid or grants to meet its 
expenses from the appropriate Government or the local authority.

†684. SHRI HARIV ANSH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) the criteria adopted for engagement of nominated members in the Central 
Advisory Board of Education (CABE);
(b) the reasons behind the engagement for maximum people of similar thought; 
and
(c) whether Government is going forward to bring changes in the education 
policy of the country and if so, the level at which the suggestions have been sought 
from the educationists for changes?   
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

394 Written Ans. to Std. and [RAJYA SABHA] Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SMRITI 
ZUBIN IRANI): (a) and (b) Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) has been 
reconstituted vide Resolution dated 11.06.2015 for a period of three years from the 
date of notification. Members representing different interests viz a viz  industry, special 
interest (SC/ST/PWD), minority institutions and eminent educationists, technologists, 
scientists, experts in school education/creative arts/languages etc. are nominated on 
CABE in order to facilitate decisions keeping in view the interests of all groups.
(c) The Government has initiated the process of formulating a New Education 
Policy to meet the changing dynamics of the population’s requirement with regard 
to quality education, innovation and research, aiming to make India a knowledge 
superpower by equipping its students with the necessary skills and knowledge and to 
eliminate the shortage of manpower in science, technology, academics and industry. 
Multiple level consultative processes involving all stakeholders, such as, educationists, 
teachers, and students across all levels are envisaged. The online consultation 
process has already been launched on www.MyGov.in portal and a huge number of 
suggestions have already been received on 33 identified themes that are accessible on  
www.MyGov.in portal. The grass roots level consultation from the Gram Panchayat 
level through the Block and District to State level is also proposed to be started 
shortly. Suggestions have also been invited from educationists from all over the 
country in this regard.
Doing away with no-detention policy
685. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that many State Governments have demanded doing 
away with no-detention policy till class VIII; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government’s reaction thereto?
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SMRITI 
ZUBIN IRANI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. From time to time, some State Governments 
have written to the Central Government to re-examine the no-detention provision 
of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009. In 
this background, the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE), in its 59th 
meeting held on 6th June, 2012, constituted a Sub-committee for assessment of 
implementation of Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE) in the context 
of no-detention provision in the RTE Act, 2009. The Sub-committee has submitted 
its report in August, 2014. The recommendations of Sub-committee include,  

Written Ans. to Std. and [30 July, 2015]   Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015 395
inter-alia, measuring learning level outcomes of all children on regular basis, to 
catalyse a performance-driven culture. The Committee has also recommended a review 
of ‘No-Detention Policy’ and its implementation in a phased manner.
Improvement of Government schools
686. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether Government has put in place a roadmap for improving the performance 
and educational standards of Government schools in Maharashtra and rest of the 
country within a time-frame and if so, the details thereof; and
(b) if not, the reasons therefor and by when Government proposes to have such 
a roadmap in place?
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SMRITI 
ZUBIN IRANI): (a) and (b) The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education 
(RTE) Act, 2009 provides a legally enforceable rights framework with targets and 
time frames. Maharashtra has notified its own State rules for RTE and hence the 
time lines are binding on the State. 
In order to improve the performance and educational standards, the Central 
Government through Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) has supported all States/UTs 
including Maharashtra on early grade reading, writing and comprehension, and early 
mathematics programmes through a sub-programme namely ‘Padhe Bharat Badhe 
Bharat’, and at upper primary level for Mathematics and Science teaching learning 
in 2014-15.
The Ministry has launched Rashtriya Aavishkar Abhiyan (RAA) Programme 
on 09.07.2015, inter-alia, as a sub-component of SSA and Rashtriya Madhyamik 
Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA), to motivate and engage children of the age group 6-18 
years in Science, Mathematics and Technology through observation, experimentation, 
inference drawing, model building, etc. both through inside and outside classroom 
activities and processes.
In addition under SSA Programme, a total of 19.78 lakh teacher posts have been 
sanctioned, against which 15.59 lakh teacher posts have been filled up by States/UTs, 
upto 31.03.2015 to improve pupil teacher ratios, imparting of regular annual-in-service 
teacher training to all teachers to update their skills and knowledge, distribution of 
free textbooks to children and providing on-site academic support to teachers through 
Block Resource Centres and Cluster Resource Centres. States/UTs have also been 
assisted to conduct comprehensive external student assessment surveys to access gaps

in student learning, in order to undertake corrective action. Under Computer Aided 
Learning (CAL) component of SSA, States/UTs have been supported financially to 
promote e-learning of Science and Mathematics at Upper Primary Level.

Introduction of CBCS
689. DR. R. LAKSHMANAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether Government has decided to introduce Choice Based Credit System 
(CBCS) in all universities throughout the country;
(b) if so, the reasons therefor;
(c) how CBCS would be different from the existing teaching learning process; 
and
(d) the details of the universities which have introduced CBCS, State-wise?
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SMRITI 
ZUBIN IRANI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Under Choice Based Credit System (CBCS) 
the availability of elective subjects increases and the student is not held hostage to 
academic inflexibility. This enables students to take courses of their choice, learn 
at their own pace, undergo additional courses and acquire more than the required 
credits, and adopt an inter-disciplinary approach to learning. The UGC has informed 
that introduction of CBCS will help resolve various difficulties faced by the students 
due to the diversity in evaluation system followed by different universities in India. 
Further, CBCS would ensure seamless mobility of students across the higher education 
institutions in the country as well as abroad where such system is a norm.

Written Ans. to Std. and [30 July, 2015]   Ustd. Ques. of 27 July, 2015 399
(c) The UGC has informed that the CBCS would be different from the existing 
teaching-learning process as it would be based on modularized semester system leading 
to the award of credits. In addition, the performance of students will be adjudged in 
terms of grades rather than numerical marks. Further, it would also provide greater 
choices to the prospective students as they may be able to earn credits in their 
chosen subjects from across the departments as also from across the institutions.
The UGC has further informed that under CBCS, universities are requested to 
shift from numerical marking system, which is followed presently in universities, to 
grading system of evaluation. The grading system is considered to be better than 
the conventional marks system and hence it has been followed in the top institutions 
in India and abroad. This will facilitate student mobility across institutions within 
and across countries and also enable potential employers to assess the performance 
of students.
Further, under CBCS, universities will move from the Conventional Annual 
System to semester system. The semester system accelerates the teaching-learning 
process and enables vertical and horizontal mobility in learning. The credit based 
semester system provides flexibility in assigning credits based on the course content 
and hours of teaching.  
The guidelines issued by UGC are available at http://www.ugc.ac.in/pdfnews/ 
9555132_Guidelines.pdf
(d) The UGC has informed that all the 39 Central Universities, funded by the 
UGC, are going to implement the Choice Based Credit System from the ensuing 
academic session. In addition, 21 State Public Universities, 5 State Private Universities 
and 6 Deemed to be Universities have also expressed their readiness for implementing 
CBCS. Details of Universities, State-wise, which have expressed their readiness for 
introducing CBCS, are given in the Statement.

Level of literacy in rural areas
696. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Ministry has taken note of the findings of the latest Socio 
Economic and Caste Census which States that out of 35.73 per cent adult literates 
in rural India, 13.9 per cent have recorded below primary level of literacy; 
(b) the details of total expenditure of the Ministry on literacy initiatives during 
the last three decades; 
(c) whether the Ministry recognizes that despite 68 years since Independence 
and crores of rupees being spent, literacy level have remained extremely low; and 
(d) the steps being taken by the Ministry to raise literacy level?
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SMRITI 
ZUBIN IRANI): (a) Socio Economic Caste Census, 2011, reported 35.73 per cent 
illiterates and 13.9 per cent literates below primary levels in rural areas of the country. 
However, Census 2011 reported 32.23 per cent illiterates in rural area. As per Census, 
a person aged 7 and above who can both read and write with understanding in any 
language is considered as literate.
(b) and (c) The details indicating plan-wise expenditure on elementary education 
and adult education from VIth Five Year Plan (1980-85) to XIth Five Year Plan 
(2007-12) are given in the Statement ( See below). As per Census reports, there has 
been steady improvement in literacy rates since independence as the literacy rate has 
increased from 18.33 per cent in 1951 to 72.98 per cent in 2011.
(d) Two major interventions of Government of India, namely Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan, for Universalisation of Elementary Education and Saakshar Bharat, a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme for the Adult population help to bring effective improvement in 
literacy. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is being implemented for Universalisation 
of Elementary Education for all children in the 6-14 age group. Saakshar Bharat 
is being implemented in rural areas of 410 districts in 26 States and one Union 
Territory (UT) that had adult female literacy rate of 50 per cent or below as per 
Census 2001 and left wing extremism affected districts, irrespective of their literacy 
rates. The Scheme has a target of making 70 million adult non-literates, including 
60 million women as literates, with special thrust on disadvantaged groups.
